# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 86 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 86 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_086_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 9 — The Tower Is Tested

**1** I watched a tall man arrive and summon the virgins, then walk around the tower inspecting it with great care. He handed a rod to the virgins, and they began striking the tower with it. **2** The whole tower shuddered, and the flawed sections broke away and fell. The solid sections held firm. **3** I was stunned — how could a tower built of such magnificent stones be shaken? **4** "Don't be alarmed," he told me. "The tower is being shaken so that the defective parts will fall away and what is sound will remain." **5** Then the tall man told the virgins, "Remove any defective stones from the tower and hand them to the builders." The removed stones turned out to be quite varied: some were round, smooth, and polished — they couldn't fit into the tower; others were cracked; others were rough; others were white and round — none of them were right for the building. **6** I watched the virgins pull some stones out of the tower and set them aside. Then they went to the gate and brought fresh stones to fill the gaps. **7** But some stones weren't brought from the gate at all — they stayed by the road, and those who had placed them there took them back. **8** "Those stones taken out and left by the road," he said, "especially those round ones — if they don't repent, they'll have no place in the building. But if they repent and prove themselves, they will be built back into the tower. If they refuse to repent, others will take their spots, and those round stones will be thrown away for good." **9** After I had taken all this in, the Shepherd said, "Come, let's step back a bit. When the virgins have finished the tower, I'll explain what all of this means." **10** I walked a short distance away with him, and the virgins completed the tower.

---

*PNEUMA renders the inspection and shaking as a dramatic quality-control test, emphasizing the distinction between structural integrity and defect.*
